footer.tagline: Temporary encrypted file exchange. No account. Gone after use.

hero.heading: Send a private file link that disappears.
hero.body: SealDrop encrypts files in your browser, gives you a link to share, and deletes the file after use or expiration. No account. No storage folder to manage.

howItWorks.heading: Three steps. No account.
howItWorks.step1Body: Choose a file and an expiration rule. The default is open once.
howItWorks.step2Body: SealDrop creates a link containing the decryption key in the URL fragment.
howItWorks.step3Body: The server removes the encrypted file after download limits or expiry are reached.

features.heading: Built for files that should not linger.
features.f1Body: Files and filenames are encrypted in the browser before upload.
features.f2Body: Every exchange works through links. There are no users, passwords, or profiles.
features.f3Body: Use open-once, short expiry windows, and optional delete links.
features.f4Body: Send a file directly or create a drop link so someone can send one to you.
features.f5Body: The server stores ciphertext and rounded size information, not plaintext content.
features.f6Body: Open source, self-hostable, and built on standard browser crypto.

security.heading: The server should never need to read your file.
security.body1: SealDrop uses the Web Crypto API to encrypt files before upload. The server stores encrypted blobs. Decryption keys live in URL fragments, which browsers do not send over HTTP.
security.body2: This does not make every risk disappear. File size and upload timing are visible, link access matters, and high-assurance users should review the source and served JavaScript.

verify.heading: Don't take our word for it.
verify.body: SealDrop publishes everything needed to check that the deployed client matches what's documented here.

cta.heading: Seal one file. Share one link. Move on.

send.s1Body: Select a file from your device. It loads into browser memory only. Nothing leaves your machine yet.
send.s2Title: Your browser generates a one-time key
send.s2Body: A cryptographically random 256-bit key is created locally using the Web Crypto API. It never touches a server.
send.s3Body: The file contents and filename are encrypted with AES-GCM before any network request is made. Nothing leaves unencrypted.
send.s4Body: The encrypted blob and encrypted metadata are sent to the server. The server stores bytes it cannot read.
send.s5Body: The decryption key lives in the URL fragment (the part after the #). Browsers never include fragments in HTTP requests, so the server never sees the key.
send.s6Body: When someone opens the link, their browser reads the key from the fragment and decrypts the file on their device. Nothing is sent to the server during this step.
send.s7Body: After the first download, or when the time limit is reached, the server permanently deletes the encrypted blob and its metadata record.

receive.s1Body: Your browser generates an ECDH P-256 key pair. The public key is sent to the server; the private key stays in your browser and appears only in your owner link.
receive.s2Title: Your private key stays with you
receive.s2Body: The private key appears only in your owner link's URL fragment. The server has no copy. Losing the owner link means losing the ability to decrypt received files.
receive.s3Body: The plain drop link contains only a random ID, with no keys in it. Anyone with this link can upload an encrypted file to you.
receive.s4Title: Uploaders encrypt to your public key
receive.s4Body: Each uploader's browser fetches your public key, generates a random per-file AES key, and encrypts the file with it.
receive.s5Title: The file key is wrapped to your public key
receive.s5Body: The AES file key is encrypted to you using ECDH key agreement, HKDF key derivation, and AES-KW wrapping. Only your private key can unwrap it.
receive.s6Body: The server holds the encrypted file and the wrapped key. Without your private key, neither is readable, not even by the server.
receive.s7Title: You decrypt with the owner link
receive.s7Body: Opening your owner link lets the browser extract your private key from the fragment, unwrap the file key, and decrypt the file locally.

expiry.heading: Files that can't linger.
expiry.sendBody: Open once (default), 1 hour, 1 day, or 7 days. The file is deleted as soon as the first condition is met.
expiry.receiveBody: Accept 1 file (default) or up to 3 files. Drops expire today or in 7 days, whichever comes first.
expiry.deletionBody: The encrypted blob is removed from storage and the database record is permanently erased. No backup, no recovery, no trace.

terms.title: Simple terms for a simple service.

usingService.heading: Using this service
usingService.body: SealDrop is provided free of charge and without warranty. By using it you agree to these terms. If you do not agree, do not use the service.

acceptableUse.heading: Acceptable use
acceptableUse.intro: You may not use SealDrop to upload, share, or distribute:
acceptableUse.item1: Content that is illegal in your jurisdiction or the jurisdiction where this service operates
acceptableUse.item2: Content that infringes the intellectual property rights of others
acceptableUse.item3: Malware, exploits, or tools designed to harm systems or people
acceptableUse.item4: Content that constitutes abuse, harassment, or threats toward any person

contentEncryption.heading: Content and encryption
contentEncryption.body: Files uploaded to SealDrop are end-to-end encrypted. We cannot inspect their contents. This is fundamental to the service's privacy guarantees, and it means you are solely responsible for the files you upload and share.

noWarranty.heading: No warranty
noWarranty.body: The service is provided "as is," without warranty of any kind. We do not guarantee availability, durability, or delivery. Files may be deleted earlier than their stated expiry if the service experiences technical issues. Do not use SealDrop as the sole copy of important data.

takedowns.heading: Takedowns and abuse
takedowns.body1: We reserve the right to delete files by ID in response to credible abuse reports or legal requirements, without confirming or disclosing the content of any file. Because files are end-to-end encrypted we cannot inspect their contents, but we can delete them by ID.
takedowns.body2Before: To report abuse or send a legal request, see the
takedowns.body2After: for what we can do and how to contact us.

liability.heading: Limitation of liability
liability.body: To the maximum extent permitted by applicable law, we are not liable for any loss of data, failure to deliver files, or any other damages arising from your use of this service.

changes.heading: Changes to these terms
changes.body: These terms may be updated at any time. Continued use of the service after changes constitutes acceptance of the revised terms.

abuse.title: How we handle abuse and legal requests.

whatWeCan.heading: What we can do
whatWeCan.intro: Upon receiving a credible abuse report or a valid legal request, we can:
whatWeCan.item1: Delete a file or drop by its random ID
whatWeCan.item2: Prevent new uploads to a specific drop link
whatWeCan.response: We aim to act on credible reports within 48 hours of receipt.

whatWeCannot.heading: What we cannot do
whatWeCannot.intro: SealDrop is end-to-end encrypted. This is not a legal claim — it is a technical fact. Before a file leaves a sender's device, it is encrypted with a key that only the recipient holds. The key is never transmitted to our servers. This means:
whatWeCannot.item1: We cannot inspect the contents of any file
whatWeCannot.item2: We cannot decrypt files on request
whatWeCannot.item3: We cannot identify who uploaded a file or who holds a share link
whatWeCannot.item4: We cannot confirm or deny whether a specific file ID contains certain content
whatWeCannot.note: Deleting a file by ID removes the encrypted blob and its database record. If the recipient has already downloaded the file, deletion has no effect on their copy.

whatToInclude.heading: What to include in a report
whatToInclude.intro: To allow us to act quickly, include:
whatToInclude.item1: The full URL of the file or drop link being reported (the random ID is all we need — do not include any URL fragment, as that is the private decryption key)
whatToInclude.item2: A brief description of the concern
whatToInclude.item3: For legal requests: the applicable law or order and jurisdiction

contact.heading: How to contact us
contact.body1Before: Send reports and legal requests by email to:
contact.body2: We do not maintain a bug bounty programme, but responsible disclosure of security vulnerabilities is welcome at the same address.

transparency.heading: Transparency
transparency.body1: We believe in being honest about our capabilities. Requests that ask us to do something technically impossible — such as decrypting a file or identifying a user — will receive an honest response explaining why we cannot comply. This is not a legal or policy position: it is a consequence of how the encryption works.

acceptableUse.bodyBefore: Using SealDrop to share illegal content, malware, or content that abuses or harasses others violates our
acceptableUse.bodyAfter: . We will act on credible reports within our technical capabilities.

hero.heading: The server should never read your file.

cards.encryptedBody: AES-GCM 256-bit in your browser, before a single byte leaves your device. The server receives only ciphertext.
cards.cannotReadBody: No keys, no filenames, no plaintext ever reach our servers. Even a full database leak reveals nothing readable.
cards.linkIsKeyBody: Whoever holds the share link can decrypt the file. Treat it like a password and send it via an encrypted channel.

storage.heading: What lives on the server.
stored: Approximate file size (padded to a privacy bucket)
notStored: Exact file size or chunk count
Any identifier linking you to a file

primitives.heading: What encrypts your file.
primitives.aesBody: Every file is locked with a 256-bit key and a 96-bit IV, both generated fresh per file. AES-GCM provides confidentiality and integrity: any tampering breaks decryption.
primitives.ecdhBody: In receive mode, the uploader and owner agree on a shared secret using elliptic-curve Diffie–Hellman without exchanging private keys. The result is processed via HKDF and used for AES-KW key wrapping.
primitives.webCryptoBody: All operations run in the browser's built-in, OS-sandboxed crypto engine. No third-party libraries, no CDN-loaded code. The implementation ships with your browser and is independently audited.

sizePrivacy.heading: Control what your upload size reveals.
sizePrivacy.standardBody: The last chunk of the file is padded to a 4 KB boundary. Upload size closely matches the real file size.
sizePrivacy.enhancedBody: The entire upload is padded to the next 1 MB boundary. An observer cannot distinguish files within the same megabyte.
sizePrivacy.maximumBody: The upload is padded to the nearest bucket: 10 MB, 50 MB, 100 MB, 500 MB, or 1 GB. Random data fills the gap so all files in a bucket look identical on the wire.
sizePrivacy.note: All padding uses cryptographically random fill. The real file size is stored only inside the encrypted metadata, which the server cannot read.

buildIdentity.heading: Verify what you're running.
buildIdentity.intro: The client that handles encryption is identified by its build commit.
buildIdentity.checksumsBefore: SHA-256 hashes of the deployed client bundles are published at
buildIdentity.checksumsMiddle: after each build. Download it and run
buildIdentity.checksumsAfter: against your local copy of the bundle to confirm the files match.
buildIdentity.manifestBefore: Each build also publishes a signed manifest at
buildIdentity.manifestMiddle: containing the commit, build time, and per-asset SHA-256 hashes, signed with an ECDSA key whose public half is published at
buildIdentity.manifestAfter: . Verifying the signature confirms the manifest was produced by the real build pipeline and not altered in transit.
buildIdentity.verifyBody: Open /checksums.txt, confirm the commit matches the build shown here, download the listed JavaScript and CSS assets, then compare their SHA-256 hashes. A mismatch means the deployed client is not the build described by this page.
buildIdentity.sourceBefore: The frontend client and browser crypto code are published at
buildIdentity.sourceAfter: . This repository is updated periodically rather than mirrored automatically, so the commit referenced in the signed build manifest may not match a commit in this repository — to verify a production build, compare the code itself rather than commit hashes.
buildIdentity.safeBrowsingBefore: You can also check sealdrop.io's reputation in
buildIdentity.safeBrowsingAfter: , an independent transparency report on known unsafe sites.
buildIdentity.safeUseBody: For highly sensitive files, use a trusted device and a browser profile with extensions disabled. SealDrop cannot protect against malware, a compromised OS, or a malicious browser extension.

threatModel.heading: What this protects against.
protects: Server compromise or full database dump
Passive network observer (HTTPS encrypts the transport; the payload is also encrypted)
File ID enumeration (IDs are cryptographically random)
doesNotProtect: Someone who holds the share link; that person is the intended recipient
A compromised browser or malicious extension
Traffic analysis: upload timing and transfer size are observable. Enhanced and Maximum privacy modes coarsen sizes to 1 MB or fixed buckets.
Legal takedown requests; we can delete encrypted blobs when required
Cloudflare infrastructure access; they run the compute and storage layer

protectedLinks.heading: Require an access code.
protectedLinks.intro: An optional second factor for the link itself.
protectedLinks.howItWorksBody: When you enable "Require access code", your browser generates a short human-readable code and uses it to lock the file key. Only someone with both the share link and the correct access code can decrypt the file.
protectedLinks.sendSeparatelyBody: The access code is shown to you after upload. Send it via a different channel than the link — for example, share the link in email and the code in a text message.
protectedLinks.neverLeavesLabel: The code never leaves your browser.
protectedLinks.neverLeavesBody: The access code is used locally to derive a wrapping key via PBKDF2-SHA256. Only the wrapped key material is stored. SealDrop never sees the code.
protectedLinks.limitsBody: This helps if a link is exposed in email history, Slack, or a link preview. It does not protect against a compromised device or someone who has obtained both the link and the code.

responsibilities.heading: Security is shared.
responsibilities.intro: SealDrop handles encryption. The rest is up to you.
responsibilities.shareLinksBody: Send share links via Signal, iMessage, or another end-to-end encrypted channel. Email, Slack, and plain SMS expose the link, and the link is the key.
responsibilities.guardOwnerBody: The owner link in receive mode gives full access to all files in a drop. Never share it. If you suspect it is compromised, close the drop and create a new one.
responsibilities.deviceMattersBody: A compromised operating system or malicious browser extension can read keys in memory before encryption. SealDrop cannot protect against a device you do not control.

privacy.heading: Nothing tracked. Nothing retained.
privacy.noAccountsBody: No email, no username, no password. Files and drop links are identified only by random IDs.
privacy.noAnalyticsBody: No third-party tracking scripts, no fingerprinting, no persistent cookies. The page you load is the page you get.
privacy.cloudflareBody: SealDrop runs on Cloudflare Workers, R2, and D1. Cloudflare processes standard HTTP metadata (IP addresses, timing, headers), but never sees encryption keys or plaintext content.

whatStored.title: What this service stores
whatStored.body: SealDrop stores encrypted file blobs, encrypted filenames and MIME types, approximate file sizes, expiry timestamps, and randomly generated file and drop IDs. None of these are linked to your identity.

whatNotStored.title: What this service does not store
items: Your name, email address, or any personal identifier
URL fragments (browsers never transmit these to servers)
IP addresses beyond what Cloudflare retains in standard access logs

retention.title: Data retention
retention.body: Files are deleted automatically when their expiry condition is met: first download, time limit, or drop closure. No manual retention period applies. No backups of file content are maintained.

thirdParty.title: Third-party services
thirdParty.bodyBefore: SealDrop runs on Cloudflare infrastructure: Workers, R2 object storage, D1 database, and Pages. Cloudflare processes standard HTTP request metadata (IP addresses, request timing, headers) as part of routing and serving requests. Cloudflare does not have access to encryption keys or plaintext content. See the
thirdParty.bodyAfter: for details on what they retain.

cookies.title: Cookies and tracking
cookies.body: No tracking cookies are set. No third-party analytics or advertising scripts are loaded. No fingerprinting is performed. The only browser storage used is temporary in-memory key state during an active encryption or decryption session.

rights.title: Your rights
rights.body: Because SealDrop does not store personal data linked to your identity, there is typically nothing to access, correct, or delete on our end. If you believe we hold personal data you can be identified by, contact us and we will investigate.

changes.title: Changes to this policy
changes.body: If this policy changes materially, we will update this page. We cannot notify you by email because we do not have your email address.
